k: Robert Allen Zimmerman was born on May 24, 1941, in Duluth, Minnesota, to Abram and Beatty Zimmerman.
After his father fell ill with polio, the family moved to Hibbing, an iron-range mining town where Beatty's family lived.
After years of playing rock and roll in school bands, he graduated from Hibbing High School in 1959.
He enrolled at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis, where he immersed himself in the Dinkytown folk scene and began performing as Bob Dylan.

t: Arrives in New York and visits Woody Guthrie
k: Dylan reached New York in January 1961 and soon visited his hero Woody Guthrie, hospitalized with Huntington's disease in New Jersey, while playing Greenwich Village coffeehouses.

t: New York Times review and Columbia contract
k: Robert Shelton's glowing New York Times review of Dylan's show at Gerde's Folk City appeared in September 1961, and John Hammond signed him to Columbia Records soon after.
At his first Newport Folk Festival in July 1963 Dylan sang with Joan Baez, and the festival closed with performers joining hands for "Blowin' in the Wind" and "We Shall Overcome".
On August 28, 1963, Dylan performed at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, including "Only a Pawn in Their Game".

t: Solo tour of England, filmed for Dont Look Back
k: In the spring of 1965 Dylan toured England with an acoustic show, and D. A. Pennebaker filmed the trip for the documentary Dont Look Back, released in 1967.
On July 25, 1965, Dylan took the Newport stage backed by members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, and his short, loud electric set drew boos from part of the folk crowd.
In November 1965 Dylan quietly married Sara Lownds, a former model, in a private ceremony on Long Island.
In late July 1966 Dylan crashed his Triumph motorcycle near his home in Woodstock, New York, and afterwards stopped touring for years.

t: "Judas!" at the Manchester Free Trade Hall
k: On May 17, 1966, during his world tour with the Hawks, an audience member in Manchester shouted "Judas" at Dylan during the electric half of the show.

t: Woodstock: basement sessions with the Hawks
k: Through 1967 Dylan recorded dozens of informal songs with members of the Hawks, soon to be the Band, in the basement of a house called Big Pink near Woodstock.
On August 31, 1969, backed by the Band, he headlined the Isle of Wight Festival in England, his first full-length concert since 1966.
In June 1970 Princeton University gave him an honorary Doctor of Music degree, a day he later turned into a song on New Morning.

t: Acts in Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid
k: Dylan took a small role as a character called Alias in Sam Peckinpah's western, filmed in Mexico, and wrote its score.

t: Back on the road with the Band
k: In January and February 1974 he toured North American arenas with the Band, his first full tour since 1966, captured on the live album Before the Flood.
Starting in Plymouth, Massachusetts in October 1975, he led a travelling caravan of musicians including Joan Baez and Roger McGuinn at first through smaller halls in New England and Canada.
He spent most of 1978 touring Japan, Australia, Europe and North America with a large band and backing singers, recording the live album At Budokan in Tokyo.

t: Saturday Night Live: three gospel songs
k: On October 20, 1979, he played three songs from Slow Train Coming as the musical guest on Saturday Night Live.
Starting November 1, 1979, he played a run of concerts at San Francisco's Fox Warfield Theatre made up only of new religious songs and none of his older hits.
In February 1980 he won the Grammy for Best Rock Vocal Performance, Male, for Gotta Serve Somebody and performed the song at the ceremony.

t: Older songs return to the set
k: In November 1980 he returned to the Warfield for shows that brought some of his older songs back alongside the gospel material.

t: Live Aid: closes the Philadelphia show
k: On July 13, 1985, Dylan played near the end of the Live Aid concert at JFK Stadium in Philadelphia, backed by Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood.

t: Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
k: Dylan was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in January 1988, with Bruce Springsteen giving the induction speech.
On June 7, 1988, in Concord, California, Dylan began the run of near-continuous touring that fans came to call the Never Ending Tour.
Dylan joined George Harrison, Jeff Lynne, Roy Orbison and Tom Petty in the Traveling Wilburys, whose first album came out in October 1988.

t: 30th anniversary concert at Madison Square Garden
k: On October 16, 1992, a host of artists performed his songs at Madison Square Garden to mark thirty years since his first album, and Dylan closed the night himself.

t: Sings at the Clinton inaugural celebration
k: In January 1993 Dylan performed Chimes of Freedom at a concert at the Lincoln Memorial celebrating Bill Clinton's inauguration.

t: Album of the Year Grammy for Time Out of Mind
k: In February 1998 Time Out of Mind won the Grammy for Album of the Year, along with two other awards that night.

t: Academy Award for Things Have Changed
k: Dylan won the Oscar for Best Original Song for Things Have Changed, written for the film Wonder Boys; it also took the Golden Globe.
Dylan's memoir Chronicles: Volume One came out in October 2004 and became a bestseller praised by critics.
President Barack Obama awarded Dylan the Presidential Medal of Freedom at the White House in May 2012.
Honored by MusiCares in Los Angeles, he gave a long, rare speech about his songwriting and his critics.
The Swedish Academy named him the 2016 laureate for creating new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition, making him the first songwriter to receive it.
He met the Nobel requirement in June 2017 by sending a recorded lecture on the books and songs that shaped him.
In March 2020, early in the pandemic, he released a seventeen-minute song about the Kennedy assassination without warning, his first new original song in eight years.
In December 2020 he sold the rights to his entire songwriting catalog to Universal Music Publishing Group.
In July 2021 he presented Shadow Kingdom, a filmed concert of reworked older songs streamed online.
He published a book of essays on dozens of songs by other artists, his first book of new prose since Chronicles: Volume One in 2004.
